newsitem.title: SYRIA: Eight Arab ministers support common market.
newsitem.headline: Eight Arab ministers support common market.

text.p: The foreign ministers of Syria, Egypt and and the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) opened talks Tuesday by voicing support for the formation of a common Arab market.

The minister of the so-called "Damascus Declaration" will also discuss during their talks at this resort, some 200 miles from Damascus, how to revive stalled Arab-Israeli peace talks and other regional issues.
Conference sources said Syria's decision to open its borders with Iraq for trade would also be tackled by the ministers.
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Saud al-Faisal, whose country is the largest oil exporter, said the kingdom supports the establishment of a common market among the eight states.

"The kingdom calls for cooperation amongst Arab states, especially in the economic field and we support the establishment of this market. We will discuss with an open heart and mind this issue," he said.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, also speaking to reporters before the meeting, said the eight ministers would discuss how to boost cooperation by forming a common market or establishing free trade zones.

"The common market was discussed by the Arab summit held in Cairo last year and the Arab League promoted the idea. The Syrian-Egyptian higher committee supported the idea during its meeting held in Cairo recently," he said.
The GCC groups Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates
Conference sources said faltering Arab-Israeli peace talks would be discussed by the ministers who are expected to suppport Syria's demands for the resumption of peace talks with Israel.
Israel broke off the talks and none have been held since rightist Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took office in June 1996.

Syria has long demanded an Israeli pullout from the Golan Heights captured in the 1967 Six-Day War between Israel and Arab neighbors. Damascus has blasted Netanyahu for his refusal to swap occupied Arab lands for a final peace agreement.

Officials said earlier the ministers would discuss Turkey's incursion into northern Iraq against the Kurds and its military cooperation with Israel, which has also raised concern among the Arab states.
